title: Quiz 1: Relational Databases, SQL and MySQL Data Types
description: 86 questions on tables, rows and columns, primary and foreign keys, indexes, views and routines, basic SELECT and JOIN queries, the system catalog, and choosing MySQL data types.

questions.question: What does a relational database management system store its data in?
options: Tables made of rows and columns, related through keys
Flat files, one per record, linked by file names
Hierarchies of parent and child nodes, linked by paths
Documents of nested fields, linked by embedded copies
questions.explanation: An RDBMS holds everything in tables. Relationships between tables are expressed with primary and foreign keys, not with file names, hierarchies or embedded documents.

questions.question: In the formal relational vocabulary, which term names a single row of a table?
options: Attribute
Tuple
Relation
Domain
questions.explanation: A tuple is a row (a record). An attribute is a column (a field), and a relation is the table itself.

questions.question: In the formal relational vocabulary, which term names a column?
options: Tuple
Relation
Attribute
Schema
questions.explanation: An attribute is a column or field. The informal terms are column or field; the non-relational equivalent is a field.

questions.question: A table of library members has a row for every member. Which formal term describes the whole table?
options: Tuple (or record)
Attribute (or field)
Index (or key)
Relation (or entity)
questions.explanation: The table as a whole is a relation, also called an entity. Its rows are tuples and its columns are attributes.

questions.question: Match each informal term to its formal relational equivalent.
questions.explanation: Informally we say table, column and row; formally they are relation, attribute and tuple.

questions.question: Which statement about a relational table is true?
options: Each row holds exactly one value for each column
A single column may hold a mix of text and numbers
Rows must be stored in order of their creation date
A cell may hold a list of several values at once
questions.explanation: Every cell holds one value, and all values in a column share one type. The order of rows and columns carries no meaning.

questions.question: In a relational table, swapping the order of two rows changes the meaning of the data.
questions.explanation: The order of rows (and of columns) has no significance. Meaning comes from the values and the keys, not from position.

questions.question: Every value stored in one column of a table must have the same data type.
questions.explanation: Each column is assigned a datatype such as integer, text or date, and every value in that column must fit it.

questions.question: A clinic stores patients, appointments and doctors. Why is each kind of information kept in its own table?
options: It forces every query to read a smaller number of columns
It removes redundancy, so a fact is entered once and stays consistent
It lets each table use a different database engine for speed
It makes sure no two tables can ever share a key value
questions.explanation: A table about one subject means a patient's details are typed once and referenced elsewhere, avoiding duplicated and conflicting copies.

questions.question: Two departments both look up customer details. In a well-designed relational database, how is that customer data held?
options: Copied into one table per department so each owns its data
Stored in a spreadsheet that each department edits locally
Entered once in a single customer table that both departments query
Typed into every order row so no join is ever needed
questions.explanation: Keeping one authoritative copy avoids inconsistencies between departments' versions.

questions.question: A row in a non-relational file system corresponds to which relational term?
options: An attribute, also called a field
A relation, also called a file
A key, also called an index
A tuple, also called a record
questions.explanation: Record and row are the same idea: record in a file, row or tuple in a table.

questions.question: Each column in a table is assigned a specific ____ such as integer, text or date. (one word)
questions.explanation: The datatype tells the database how to store, validate and compare the values in the column.

questions.question: What is the job of a primary key?
options: To identify each row in the table uniquely
To point at a row stored in a different table
To speed up every query that reads the table
To restrict which users may change the table
questions.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies a row. Pointing to another table is the job of a foreign key.

questions.question: Which pair of rules must every primary key value obey?
options: It must be numeric and it must be auto-generated
It must be unique and it must not be NULL
It must be short and it must never be changed
It must be sorted and it must start at the value 1
questions.explanation: Uniqueness and NOT NULL are the two mandatory properties. Numeric, short or auto-generated keys are common practice, not rules.

questions.question: What does a foreign key do?
options: Stores a value that must be unique across its own table
Stores a copy of every column from a related table
Stores a value that refers to the primary key of a related table
Stores a value that is calculated from other columns
questions.explanation: A foreign key value is a reference to the associated table's primary key, which is how rows in two tables are related.

questions.question: A foreign key column may be given a different name from the primary key it refers to.
questions.explanation: Matching names are common, but what matters is that the values refer to the primary key of the referenced table.

questions.question: A table in a relational database is allowed to have no primary key at all.
questions.explanation: Every table must have a primary key. If none is declared, all the columns together act as the key.

questions.question: A shipment table has shipment_id as its primary key and warehouse_id as a foreign key to the warehouse table. Which table is the referencing table?
options: warehouse, because it holds the foreign key
shipment, because it holds the referenced key
warehouse, because it holds the referenced key
shipment, because it holds the foreign key
questions.explanation: The table containing the foreign key is the referencing (foreign) table; the table containing the primary key it points to is the referenced (primary) table.

questions.question: A shipment table has shipment_id as its primary key and warehouse_id as a foreign key to the warehouse table. Which table is the referenced table?
options: warehouse, because it holds the primary key being pointed to
shipment, because it holds the primary key being pointed to
warehouse, because it holds the foreign key doing the pointing
shipment, because it holds the foreign key doing the pointing
questions.explanation: The referenced (primary) table is the one whose primary key the foreign key refers to.

questions.question: A table lists which student enrolled in which section. Neither student_id nor section_id is unique alone, but each pair appears once. What kind of primary key is needed?
options: A surrogate key made of a single auto-numbered column
A composite key made of student_id and section_id together
A foreign key made of student_id and section_id together
A candidate key made of the student's name and section
questions.explanation: When one column cannot identify a row but a combination can, the primary key is composite (composed of more than one column).

questions.question: If a table has no primary key declared, the database treats all of its columns together as the key.
questions.explanation: With no primary key assigned, the full set of columns becomes the key, which is why a compact, deliberate key is better practice.

questions.question: Which primary key is best practice?
options: One that combines every column that could ever be unique
One that holds descriptive text so rows are readable
One that is as compact as possible
One that is recalculated whenever the row is updated
questions.explanation: Compact keys keep indexes small and joins fast. A key built from many or wide columns costs space and speed.

questions.question: In a table of order lines, the columns are order_id, product_id, quantity and ship_date. A given product can appear once per order. What is the natural primary key?
options: order_id alone, since it names the order
product_id alone, since it names the item
quantity and ship_date together, since they vary
order_id and product_id together
questions.explanation: A single order has several lines, and a product appears on many orders, so only the pair order_id + product_id identifies one line.

questions.question: In an orders table, customer_id holds the value 7, and no customer 7 exists in the customer table. What has gone wrong?
options: The foreign key refers to a primary key value that is not there
The primary key of the customer table has been duplicated
The primary key of the orders table has become NULL
The two tables have been joined on the wrong data type
questions.explanation: A foreign key value must match an existing primary key value in the referenced table, otherwise the relationship is broken (an orphan row).

questions.question: In the example where order 3 has customer_id 1 and customer 1 is Joe Smith, what does that foreign key value tell you?
options: Joe Smith placed three orders in total
Order 3 belongs to Joe Smith
Order 1 belongs to the third customer
Joe Smith is the first row in the order table
questions.explanation: The foreign key links the order to the customer row whose primary key has that value.

questions.question: A primary key made of more than one column is called a ____ key. (one word)
questions.explanation: A composite primary key is 'composed' of two or more columns.

questions.question: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Uniquely identifies each row; never NULL
Refers to a row in another table
A primary key built from several columns
The table whose primary key is pointed to

questions.explanation: Keys define the relational structure: how rows are identified and how tables relate.

questions.question: How is a database index best compared to something familiar?
options: The table of contents at the front that lists each chapter in reading order
The glossary at the back that defines each term in plain everyday language
The index at the back of a book that lists the pages for each term
The appendix at the back that adds extra material for further reading and study
questions.explanation: An index relates each indexed value to the physical location of the matching rows, just as a book index maps terms to pages.

questions.question: What is the main reason to create an index on a column?
options: To prevent users from reading the column's values directly
To store a second copy of the table for backup purposes
To make the column's values unique across the whole table
To let the database find rows by that column's value quickly
questions.explanation: Indexes are a performance design element for fast lookup. Backup and uniqueness are different features.

questions.question: Indexes are transparent to the user: a query is written the same way whether or not an index exists.
questions.explanation: The database decides when to use an index. Users and applications do not reference it in their queries.

questions.question: What is a view?
options: A virtual table whose rows are computed from underlying tables when it is used
A stored copy of a table that is refreshed automatically each night
A special table that records every change made to its rows over time
A fast lookup structure that points to where matching rows are stored
questions.explanation: A view looks like a table to applications but holds no data of its own; its contents are computed from base tables each time.

questions.question: What are the tables that actually hold the data called, to tell them apart from views?
options: Parent tables
Base tables
Index tables
Master tables
questions.explanation: Base tables store the information; views are computed from them.

questions.question: A view stores its own copy of the rows it displays.
questions.explanation: A view does not hold data. Whenever it is accessed, its rows are computed from the underlying tables.

questions.question: What is a stored procedure?
options: A query result saved inside the database so it can be reused by many users
A backup job saved inside the database that runs on a nightly schedule
A routine saved inside the database that can take parameters and run queries
A security rule saved inside the database that limits access to tables
questions.explanation: Stored procedures are named routines held in the database itself, which can accept parameters such as a minimum spend.

questions.question: What makes a trigger different from an ordinary stored procedure?
options: It runs only when an administrator schedules it to run overnight each day
It runs only when a user calls it by name and passes the required parameters
It fires automatically whenever the database server is stopped or restarted
It fires automatically when data in its table is inserted, updated or deleted
questions.explanation: A trigger is a special stored procedure tied to a table; it runs on its own when a matching change happens.

questions.question: A business rule says that every time a row is removed from the staff table, a record of the removal must be written to an audit table. Which object suits this best?
options: A trigger on the staff table
A view over the staff table
An index on the staff table
A composite key on the staff table
questions.explanation: Triggers automatically maintain business rules when data changes. A view, index or key does not run actions.

questions.question: A manager wants a reusable routine that returns every customer who has spent more than an amount she supplies each time. Which object fits?
options: A trigger that fires on every insert into the customer table
A stored procedure with a parameter for the amount
An index on the column that holds the spending total
A view with the amount written in its definition
questions.explanation: Stored procedures can take parameters, so one routine can serve many different thresholds.

questions.question: Match each database object to what it is for.

pairs.right: Fast lookup of rows by value
A virtual table computed from base tables
A saved routine that can take parameters
A routine that fires on insert, update or delete

sections.name: 4. SQL Queries and the System Catalog

questions.category: SQL Queries and the System Catalog
questions.question: Which SQL statement retrieves data from a table?
options: INSERT
UPDATE
SELECT
CREATE
questions.explanation: SELECT reads data. INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes them, and CREATE builds objects such as tables.

questions.category: SQL Queries and the System Catalog
questions.question: In SELECT title, price FROM book WHERE price > 15; what does the WHERE clause do?
options: It keeps only the columns whose name is above 15
It sorts the rows so the prices above 15 come first
It adds 15 to the price in each row it returns
It keeps only the rows whose price is above 15
questions.explanation: WHERE is a restriction (filter) on rows. The column list after SELECT controls which columns come back.

questions.category: SQL Queries and the System Catalog
questions.question: In SELECT title, price FROM book WHERE price > 15; which part chooses the columns that are returned?
options: title, price
FROM book
WHERE price > 15
price > 15
questions.explanation: The list after SELECT names the columns. FROM names the table and WHERE filters rows.

questions.category: SQL Queries and the System Catalog
questions.question: What does a JOIN do?
options: Copies all of the rows from one table into a second table in the database
Links rows from two or more tables by comparing values in key columns
Merges two tables into one new permanent table stored in the database
Combines the columns of one table into a single text value in the output
questions.explanation: A join returns rows with matching key values (such as PK and FK) as a result; it does not change the stored tables.

questions.category: SQL Queries and the System Catalog
questions.question: A JOIN permanently merges the two tables it reads into a single new table.
questions.explanation: A join only produces a result set. The underlying tables are unchanged.

questions.category: SQL Queries and the System Catalog
questions.question: A query joins orders and customers. Which columns would you normally compare?
options: The two primary keys of the tables being joined
The first column that appears in each of the tables
The foreign key in orders and the primary key in customers
The two columns that happen to have the same type
questions.explanation: Joins follow the relationship: the FK in one table is matched with the PK it refers to.

questions.category: SQL Queries and the System Catalog
questions.question: Which statement removes existing rows from a table?
options: DROP
REMOVE
ALTER
DELETE
questions.explanation: DELETE removes rows. DROP removes a whole object such as a table, and ALTER changes a table's structure.

questions.category: SQL Queries and the System Catalog
questions.question: Besides retrieving data, which tasks does SQL cover?
options: Inserting, updating and deleting rows, and creating or dropping objects
Designing screens, printing reports, and scheduling nightly backups of files
Compiling programs, installing software, and managing the files on a disk
Encrypting disks, routing traffic, and monitoring the health of networks
questions.explanation: SQL is also used for data changes and for defining objects such as tables and views.

questions.category: SQL Queries and the System Catalog
questions.question: What are system tables, also called the data dictionary or system catalog?
options: Tables that store the business data for the applications built on top of the database
Special tables the system uses to hold information about the database itself
Tables that each user creates to keep their own private working notes and scratch data
Tables that hold backup copies of the user tables so they can be recovered
questions.explanation: System tables describe the database: its tables, users and columns.

questions.category: SQL Queries and the System Catalog
questions.question: Which is an example of metadata that the system catalog would hold?
options: The total sales figure for last month
The phone number of a particular customer
The list of column names and data types in a table
The price of one product on a given day
questions.explanation: Metadata is data about data. A column's name and type describe the table; sales, phone numbers and prices are ordinary data.

questions.category: SQL Queries and the System Catalog
questions.question: You should alter the system tables directly, in the same way that you update your own tables.
questions.explanation: System tables are managed by the database. You read them but never alter them directly.

questions.category: SQL Queries and the System Catalog
questions.question: Data about data, such as the names of a table's columns, is called ____. (one word)
questions.explanation: Metadata is the information the system tables keep about tables, columns and users.

questions.category: SQL Queries and the System Catalog
questions.question: Show the given_name and hourly_rate of every steward who earns more than 20 per hour.
questions.solution: SELECT given_name, hourly_rate FROM steward WHERE hourly_rate > 20;
questions.explanation: Name the two columns after SELECT and filter rows with WHERE.

questions.category: SQL Queries and the System Catalog
questions.question: List the title and daily fee of every gadget whose daily fee is under 3.
questions.solution: SELECT gadget_title, daily_fee FROM gadget WHERE daily_fee < 3;
questions.explanation: A filter on a numeric column; only the two named columns are returned.

questions.category: SQL Queries and the System Catalog
questions.question: Show each gadget's title together with the name of its maker. Join gadget and maker on maker_id.
questions.solution: SELECT gadget.gadget_title, maker.maker_name FROM gadget JOIN maker ON gadget.maker_id = maker.maker_id;
questions.explanation: gadget.maker_id is the foreign key and maker.maker_id is the primary key it refers to.

questions.category: SQL Queries and the System Catalog
questions.question: Show every locality's name with its region's name, by joining locality and region on region_id.
questions.solution: SELECT locality.locality_name, region.region_name FROM locality JOIN region ON locality.region_id = region.region_id;
questions.explanation: A join across a foreign key: locality.region_id refers to region.region_id.

questions.question: Why does a database column need a declared data type at all?
options: The same bits take up less disk space once a type has been declared for them
The same bits can only be read by the single user who first created them
The same bits stay encrypted on disk until a type has been declared for them
The same bits can mean a number, text or a date, and the type says which
questions.explanation: A type is the contract that tells MySQL how to interpret stored bits, as well as how much space to reserve and what operations are valid.

questions.question: Which is a benefit of declaring a correct data type, other than interpretation?
options: It rejects nonsense, such as text in a column meant for ages
It makes every column in the table unique and not null
It lets two columns hold different types in the same row
It turns every value into text before it is stored
questions.explanation: Types give free validation, proper sorting and math, and date arithmetic.

questions.question: A column holds quantities from 0 to 200 and never goes negative. Which numeric type is the smallest that fits?
options: SMALLINT UNSIGNED
TINYINT UNSIGNED
MEDIUMINT UNSIGNED
INT UNSIGNED
questions.explanation: TINYINT is one byte and UNSIGNED gives it a range of 0 to 255, which covers 200. Larger integer types waste space.

questions.question: Which integer type uses 4 bytes and is the default workhorse integer?
options: TINYINT
MEDIUMINT
INT
BIGINT
questions.explanation: INT is 4 bytes and covers about ±2.1 billion. BIGINT is 8 bytes, MEDIUMINT 3, TINYINT 1.

questions.question: A table is expected to hold more than ten billion rows, each with an auto-numbered ID. Which type should the ID use?
options: INT
MEDIUMINT
DECIMAL(5,2)
BIGINT
questions.explanation: INT tops out near 2.1 billion (4.3 billion unsigned). BIGINT has room for IDs far beyond that.

questions.question: Match each integer type to its storage size.
What does adding UNSIGNED to an integer column do?
options: Allows no negative values, which doubles the positive range
Allows only negative values, which doubles the negative range
Allows decimal places, which doubles the number of digits
Allows NULL values, which doubles the number of states
questions.explanation: The same number of bits is used for non-negative values only, so the maximum doubles.

questions.question: Which type should hold a product price in a shop's database?
options: FLOAT
DECIMAL(8,2)
DOUBLE
BIT(8)
questions.explanation: DECIMAL is exact fixed-point, so money is not subject to rounding. FLOAT and DOUBLE are approximate.

questions.question: Why should FLOAT and DOUBLE be avoided for currency?
options: They store only whole numbers, so any cents in a price would be lost entirely
They store text values, so they cannot be added together in a query at all
They store approximate values, so sums such as 0.1 + 0.2 may not equal 0.3
They store negative values only, so every total would come out wrong and negative
questions.explanation: Floating point types are fast but imprecise. DECIMAL is the exact choice for money.

questions.question: DECIMAL(M,D) stores exact values, so it is the right choice when rounding errors are not acceptable.
questions.explanation: DECIMAL is exact fixed-point: M is the total digits and D the digits after the decimal point.

questions.question: Which type is meant for a true or false flag?
options: BIT(8), which is stored as eight characters of text
TINYTEXT, which is stored as the words true or false
DECIMAL(1,0), which is stored as a fixed-point digit
BOOLEAN, which is stored as 1 for true and 0 for false
questions.explanation: BOOLEAN (BOOL) is one byte holding 1 or 0. TINYINT is used the same way in practice.

questions.question: What is the difference between CHAR(10) and VARCHAR(10)?
options: CHAR pads values to a fixed length; VARCHAR stores only the length used
CHAR stores only the length used; VARCHAR pads to a fixed length
CHAR holds numbers only; VARCHAR holds letters and symbols too
CHAR holds up to ten bytes; VARCHAR holds up to ten thousand
questions.explanation: CHAR(N) is fixed length and suits uniform values such as codes. VARCHAR(N) is variable length.

questions.question: A column holds two-letter state abbreviations such as TX and OH. Which type fits best?
options: TEXT
CHAR(2)
VARCHAR(255)
BLOB
questions.explanation: A uniform, fixed-length value is where CHAR is a good fit. TEXT and BLOB are for large or binary content.

questions.question: A column holds customer last names that vary from 2 to 40 characters. Which type is the safe default?
options: CHAR(50)
LONGTEXT
VARCHAR(50)
ENUM('short','long')
questions.explanation: VARCHAR is the default for most text because it stores only the length used.

questions.question: When is TEXT a better choice than VARCHAR?
options: When every value is the same short length each time
When the column needs to be indexed for very fast lookups
When the values are a small fixed list of allowed words
When the content may be longer than the VARCHAR limit allows
questions.explanation: Reach for TEXT only past VARCHAR limits. It indexes poorly, so it is a poor choice for short, searchable values.

questions.question: Which type family holds binary large objects such as images and files?
options: BLOB
TEXT
ENUM
VARBINARY(20)
questions.explanation: BLOB types store raw bytes of any size up to their limit. TEXT is for character data.

questions.question: A column must hold exactly one of 'bronze', 'silver' or 'gold'. Which type is compact and self-validating?
options: SET('bronze','silver','gold')
ENUM('bronze','silver','gold')
TINYTEXT
VARCHAR(255)
questions.explanation: ENUM allows one value from a fixed list. SET allows zero or more, so it would permit combinations.

questions.question: A column records which days of the week a class meets, and a class can meet on several days. Which type is designed for this?
options: ENUM('Mon','Tue','Wed','Thu','Fri')
CHAR(5)
SET('Mon','Tue','Wed','Thu','Fri')
TINYINT UNSIGNED
questions.explanation: SET stores zero or more values from a predefined list. ENUM holds just one.

questions.question: ENUM is a good choice for values that change often, because new options can be added without altering the table.
questions.explanation: ENUM suits a known, fixed set but is painful to alter later, since adding a value means changing the column definition.

questions.question: With the utf8mb4 character set, what should you keep in mind when sizing text columns?
options: A single character always takes exactly 1 byte
A single character takes at most 2 bytes
A single character takes a variable number of bits
A single character can take up to 4 bytes
questions.explanation: utf8mb4 uses up to 4 bytes per character, so byte limits and index sizes need attention.

questions.question: Which DATE range and format does MySQL use?
options: YYYY-MM-DD, covering years 1000 through 9999
DD-MM-YYYY, covering years 1000 through 9999
YYYY-MM-DD, covering years 1970 through 2038
MM/DD/YYYY, covering years 0001 through 9999
questions.explanation: DATE is 3 bytes in YYYY-MM-DD format. 1970 to 2038 is the TIMESTAMP range.

questions.question: Which of these can represent a duration longer than 24 hours, such as 90:30:00?
options: DATE
TIME
YEAR
TIMESTAMP
questions.explanation: TIME stores HH:MM:SS and, unlike a clock time, can also hold durations beyond a day.

questions.question: What is the difference between DATETIME and TIMESTAMP?
options: DATETIME is stored as UTC and converted to the session time zone; TIMESTAMP is not converted
TIMESTAMP stores a date only; DATETIME stores a date and a time together
TIMESTAMP is stored as UTC and converted to the session time zone; DATETIME is not converted
DATETIME is limited to years 1970 to 2038; TIMESTAMP covers years 1000 to 9999
questions.explanation: TIMESTAMP is 4 bytes, UTC based and limited to 1970-2038. DATETIME is 5 bytes, has a wider range and stores the literal value.

questions.question: A system must store birth dates of historical figures born in the 1700s. Which type works?
options: TIMESTAMP
TIME
YEAR
DATE
questions.explanation: TIMESTAMP starts at 1970, so it cannot hold 1700s dates. DATE covers 1000 to 9999.

questions.question: Which date type runs into a limit in the year 2038?
options: TIMESTAMP
DATETIME
DATE
YEAR
questions.explanation: TIMESTAMP is limited to 1970 through 2038; DATETIME and DATE have much wider ranges.

questions.question: Storing dates as strings such as 'March 5, 2026' is fine, because MySQL can sort them correctly.
questions.explanation: Strings lose correct sorting, validation and date arithmetic. Use a DATE, DATETIME or TIMESTAMP column.

questions.question: A table needs only the model year of a vehicle (such as 2019). Which type is the smallest?
options: DATE, at 3 bytes
YEAR, at 1 byte
TIME, at 3 bytes
DATETIME, at 5 bytes
questions.explanation: YEAR stores a year only and uses a single byte.

questions.question: What kind of data is the JSON type intended for?
options: Fixed, fully structured rows where every attribute needs a relational column of its own
Large binary files such as images that need to be stored and downloaded whole
Flexible, semi-structured documents that need validation and path-based queries
Small, repeated status codes that each need to fit in a single byte of storage
questions.explanation: JSON is a native type for structured documents. It should not replace a proper relational column when one would do.

questions.question: What is the rule of thumb for choosing a data type?
options: Pick the largest type available for each column so that no value is ever rejected by it
Pick the most general type available so that columns can be changed freely later on
Pick the very same type for every column in the table so that joins are always simpler
Pick the smallest, most specific type that still represents the data faithfully
questions.explanation: Smaller types keep indexes lean and queries fast; being specific also gives free validation.

questions.question: Match each requirement to the best type.

pairs.left: A price in dollars and cents
A photo stored in the database

questions.question: Match each date type to its description.

pairs.right: Date and time, literal value, no time zone conversion

questions.question: To store money exactly, with no rounding error, use the ____ type. (one word)
questions.explanation: DECIMAL(M,D) is exact fixed-point; FLOAT and DOUBLE are approximate.
